enonce_intro_markdown:

questions.corrige_markdown:
Take the upward direction as positive. While the ball is moving upwards, the weight $mg$ and the resistance $kmv$ both act downwards (the resistance opposes the motion). Newton's second law, with acceleration $\dfrac{dv}{dt}$:

$$
m\frac{dv}{dt} = -mg - kmv.
$$

The speed is a function of the height $x$, so by the chain rule

$$
\frac{dv}{dt} = \frac{dv}{dx}\cdot\frac{dx}{dt} = v\frac{dv}{dx}.
$$

Hence $m\,v\dfrac{dv}{dx} = -mg - kmv$. Dividing by $m$ and rearranging,

$$
v\frac{dv}{dx} + g + kv = 0.
$$

questions.enonce_markdown: the maximum height of the ball above its initial position is $\dfrac{g}{k^2}(1 - \ln 2)$. *[8 marks]*
questions.corrige_markdown:
At the initial position $x = 0$ the velocity is $v = \dfrac{g}{k}$. At the greatest height the ball is instantaneously at rest: $v = 0$. From part (i),

$$
\frac{dx}{dv} = -\frac{v}{g + kv}.
$$

Integrate between the initial state ($x = 0$, $v = g/k$) and the highest point ($x = H$, $v = 0$):

$$
H = -\int_{g/k}^{0}\frac{v}{g + kv}\,dv = \int_0^{g/k}\frac{v}{g + kv}\,dv.
$$

Write $\dfrac{v}{g + kv} = \dfrac{1}{k}\left(1 - \dfrac{g}{g + kv}\right)$. Then

$$
H = \frac{1}{k}\left[v - \frac{g}{k}\ln(g + kv)\right]_0^{g/k}
= \frac{1}{k}\left[\frac{g}{k} - \frac{g}{k}\ln(2g) + \frac{g}{k}\ln g\right]
= \frac{g}{k^2}\left[1 - \ln\frac{2g}{g}\right].
$$

$$
H = \frac{g}{k^2}\,(1 - \ln 2).
$$

Since $\ln 2 \approx 0.693 < 1$, $H > 0$, as expected.
